Fourteen hours in the car, seven days in the mountains, one
moose, one eagle and one very small fish.
We left Madison at five in the morning with a roof box, a cooler,
two children who had been promised moose and a dog who had
not been told anything. Fourteen hours later, after two states of
corn and one state of nothing at all, the mountains came up over
the dashboard and the whole car went quiet.
We rolled into town in time to stand under the antler arches on
Jackson Town Square, which Leo had been told about and did
not believe until he touched one.
Day 1. Under the antler arches on the town square. Leo counted the antlers and gave up at eleven.
Somewhere past the state line. The mountains in the window, the sun hat over the face.
Dinner was burgers and milkshakes in a diner with wooden
booths. Ivy laughed so hard at something Tom said about
cowboy hats that she got milkshake up her nose, which made it
Burgers and milkshakes to celebrate fourteen hours in the car.
The alarm went off at a quarter to five and nobody spoke to
anybody. We drove out in the dark to Mormon Row, where an
old barn stands in the sagebrush with the whole range behind it.
Then the sun came up and lit the peaks pink, one at a time, from
the top down. Ivy said it looked like someone was coloring them
Day 2, six in the morning. The old barn on Mormon Row with the whole range lit up behind it.
Tom and Ivy on the fence, watching the light come down the peaks.
Then on to Schwabacher Landing for the famous reflection.
There was no wind at all, so there were two mountain ranges,
one of them upside down. Leo found a beaver dam and
explained it to us at length.
Schwabacher Landing. No wind, no ripples, two mountain ranges.
Leo found the beaver dam and explained it to us at length.
We took the little shuttle boat across Jenny Lake instead of
walking around it, which was the right decision and the first of
Day 3. The shuttle boat across Jenny Lake, peaks close enough to touch.
From the far shore it is a short, steep climb to Hidden Falls,
which you hear long before you see. Then it keeps going up to
Inspiration Point, where the lake is suddenly a long way below
you and the boat looks like a bath toy.
Hidden Falls, which is very well hidden until it is suddenly very loud.
Inspiration Point. We were inspired, mostly to sit down.
Back at the dock, Leo took his boots off and refused to put them
back on until he had dangled his feet over the water for exactly
as long as he wanted to.
Boots off, feet over the water, back at the dock.
The trail to Taggart Lake goes through a forest of aspens with
wildflowers underneath, yellow and purple and some kind of
red one nobody could name. Three miles there and back, which
is the perfect distance for a five-year-old with snacks.
Day 4. The Taggart Lake trail, aspens and wildflowers all the way.
Taggart Lake. The clearest water any of us has ever seen.
We ate lunch on a big flat rock at the water’s edge. Ivy drew the
mountains in her notebook. On the way back we stopped at the
tiny log chapel at Moose, which has a window behind the altar
that frames the Grand Teton like a painting.
Lunch on a flat rock. Ivy drew the mountains; the mountains were better.
The little log chapel at Moose. The best window in Wyoming.
STOP 8 · SNAKE RIVER FLOAT (DEADMAN'S BAR) · 9:30 AM
The float trip put in at Snake River float (Deadman’s Bar): a big
rubber raft, life jackets for everyone, and a guide called Jen who
knew every bird by name. The river is gentle here, fast and
green, and you sit and watch the range slide past.
Day 5. Life jackets on, a guide at the oars, Deadman’s Bar behind us.

That evening we drove up to Oxbow Bend because someone at
the campground had said the word moose. There he was,
standing in the shallows like he owned the place, which I
suppose he does. We watched him for half an hour. He did not
Oxbow Bend at dinnertime. A bull moose, standing in the shallows like he owned it.
Everyone watching the moose. Biscuit was not invited, and has not forgiven us.
In the morning we drove to the top of Signal Mountain, where
the whole valley is laid out underneath you: the lake, the river,
the range, and somewhere down there our car with the roof
Day 6. The top of Signal Mountain, the whole valley laid out underneath.
Us, at the top, before the wind took Tom’s hat.
In the afternoon we rented a red canoe at Colter Bay. It took us
ten minutes to agree which way was forward. Leo caught a fish
roughly the size of his thumb and released it with a short
We spent the evening toasting marshmallows outside a log
cabin. Nobody burned theirs, which is a family first.
The red canoe on Colter Bay. Four paddles, one direction, eventually.
Leo’s fish. It was released, with a speech.
Marshmallows by the cabin. Nobody burned theirs, which is a family first.
Our last morning was at String Lake, which is shallow and clear
and so cold it makes you shout. The kids waded. Tom jumped off
a rock, against advice, and came up making a noise I have never
Day 7. String Lake, shallow and clear and freezing.
Tom, mid-jump, about half a second before he found out how freezing.
Then the Teton Village tram, four thousand feet straight up in a
red cabin, and waffles at the top, which were worth the ride on
The tram from Teton Village, four thousand feet straight up.
Waffles at the top. Worth the ride on their own.
On the way out of the park we stopped one last time at the Snake
River Overlook, the view everybody knows, and stood at the
railing for a long time without saying much.
Seven days, thirteen stops, one moose, one eagle, one very small
fish. Ivy has already asked if we can come back when she is ten.
